item.title: The math behind why young startup employees are underinsured by over Rs 1 Cr
item.description: The math behind why young startup employees are underinsured by over Rs 1 Cr Many young professionals assume their existing cover is sufficient. However, the question they need to ask is ‘how much term insurance do I need’, to adequately protect their family from outstanding liabilities and future
item.content:encoded:
Many young professionals assume their existing cover is sufficient. However, the question they need to ask is ‘how much term insurance do I need’, to adequately protect their family from outstanding liabilities and future financial goals.

A life cover of Rs 50 lakh can sound substantial at 28. You may have just received an appraisal, begun an SIP, and perhaps taken a home loan with the confidence that your career is still on an upward curve. But life cover is not meant to reflect where your income stands today alone. It needs to account for the financial responsibilities your family would have to manage if your income stopped unexpectedly.

Consider a 28-year-old startup employee earning Rs 15 lakh a year. He has Rs 50 lakh of existing cover: Rs 20 lakh through his employer and a Rs 30 lakh individual policy. On paper, he is insured. In reality, he could still have a protection gap of Rs 1.2 crore.

Why existing cover can create false comfort

Employer-provided insurance is useful, but it is usually linked to your job. If you switch companies, take a career break, or lose your job, that cover may not continue. An individual term Insurance policy is portable because it stays with you as long as you pay the premiums and meet the policy conditions.

The bigger issue is that many people choose a round figure without calculating their actual financial responsibilities. A Rs 50 lakh cover may have been enough when you were single and had no loans. It may be inadequate once you have a home loan, parents who depend on you, a spouse, or plans for children.

At 28, you also have a long earning runway ahead. Your family is not only losing your current salary if you are no longer around; they may lose the future financial support your career could have provided.

The math behind the Rs 1.2 crore gap

Here is a simple illustration for a startup employee with a monthly take-home income of about Rs 1 lakh. Assume that he contributes Rs 75,000 each month towards household expenses, savings, and family commitments.

Financial need

Income replacement for 12 years at ₹9 lakh a year - Estimated amount: ₹1.08 crore

Outstanding home loan - Estimated amount: ₹50 lakh

Support for dependent parents and medical needs - Estimated amount: ₹20 lakh

Future family goal or child’s education - Estimated amount: ₹30 lakh

Emergency reserve for the family - Estimated amount: ₹12 lakh

Total financial requirement: ₹2.20 crore

Less liquid savings and investments: ₹30 lakh

Required life cover - Estimated amount: ₹1.90 crore

Existing cover - ₹70 lakh

Protection gap - Estimated amount: ₹1.20 crore

This is only an illustration, not a universal recommendation. Your required cover will differ based on your income, debts, savings, dependants, and financial goals. Still, it shows why choosing cover based only on a familiar number can leave a major shortfall.

How much term insurance do I need? A practical calculation

The question is not simply whether you have a policy. It is how much term insurance do I need for the people and obligations that depend on me?

Start with the amount your family would need to maintain their lifestyle. Include regular expenses, loan repayments, education costs, medical support for parents, and major goals you have committed to. Then subtract assets that your family can access immediately, such as liquid savings, fixed deposits, and existing investments.

Do not count every investment at its current market value without thought. Long-term investments may be earmarked for retirement, and selling them at the wrong time can disrupt your family’s future. Similarly, do not assume your employer’s cover will always remain available.

A term insurance calculator can help you estimate the cover required by bringing these numbers together. Use realistic inputs, especially for liabilities and income replacement, rather than selecting the lowest premium shown.

Why young startup employees need to look beyond salary

Startup careers can grow quickly, but they can also change quickly. Your compensation may include variable pay, stock options, or performance-linked incentives. These elements can make you feel financially secure while leaving your family dependent on a salary that may not be easily replaced.

You may also have responsibilities that do not show up in your monthly budget. For instance, you may contribute towards a parent’s treatment, help a sibling with education, or be planning a house purchase with your partner. These commitments should be reflected in your term insurance cover.

Buying earlier can help because premiums are generally lower when you are younger and in good health. It also gives you the opportunity to secure a longer policy term before health concerns or lifestyle changes affect your eligibility or premium.

Do not use a simple salary multiple blindly

A common approach is to choose cover worth 10 or 15 times your annual income. This can be a useful starting point, but it is not the final answer. A person earning Rs 15 lakh with no debt and substantial savings may need a different cover amount from someone with the same income and a Rs 50 lakh home loan.

Instead, use salary as one input within a wider calculation. If your family needs Rs 75,000 each month, estimate how long they would need this support. Then add liabilities and future goals. Finally, reduce the total by assets that can genuinely be used by your family.

When you ask how much term insurance do I need, focus on the financial gap rather than a headline number. The goal is to ensure that your family does not have to compromise on essential needs, education, or loan repayments after an unexpected event.

What should you review before buying?

Choose a policy term that covers your highest-responsibility years. This may be until your home loan is repaid, your children become independent, or you build enough retirement savings. Also check whether your nominee would benefit more from a lump-sum payout, monthly income or a combination of both.

Disclose your health history, lifestyle habits, and occupation accurately. Incorrect or incomplete information can affect claim assessment later. Keep your nominee details current and tell your family where the policy documents are stored.

A term insurance calculator is helpful when comparing different cover amounts and policy terms. But it should support your decision, not replace a clear review of your financial responsibilities.

The real cost of waiting

The Rs 1.2 crore gap in this example is not caused by a lack of intent. It comes from delaying the calculation while responsibilities quietly increase. At 28, you may feel that a larger cover can wait until you are married, buy a home, or become a parent. By then, the premium may be higher, and the financial consequences of remaining underinsured may be greater.

The right term insurance cover should reflect the life you are building, not just the salary you receive today. Review it whenever your income, debt or family responsibilities change. That simple review can turn a policy into meaningful financial protection for the people who count on you.

(Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

item.title: 5 Lessons from Grief burns like fever by Minakshi Thakur
item.description: Explore five lessons from Minakshi Thakur’s Grief Burns Like Fever on loss, compassion, resilience and the quiet kindness that connects us.
item.content:encoded:
What happens when life changes overnight, leaving people to deal with loss, fear and uncertainty? In difficult times, some people struggle to find their way, while others discover a strength they never knew they possessed.

Grief Burns Like Fever by Minakshi Thakur explores these experiences against the backdrop of a harsh lockdown. The novel brings together the lives of an ambulance driver transporting bodies, an adolescent coping with his mother's death, a woman questioning her marriage and another trying to escape decades of captivity.

Through these interconnected stories, Thakur explores love, longing, grief and the different ways people respond to suffering.

5 Key lessons on resilience and human connection

1. Grief affects everyone differently

Losing someone or something important can change the way we see the world. While some people express their pain openly, others withdraw into themselves or struggle to understand what they are feeling.

The novel explores grief through characters facing different forms of suffering, reminding readers that there is no single way to experience loss. What helps one person cope may not work for another.

The lesson: Give yourself and others the time and space needed to process grief. Healing does not follow a fixed timeline, and nobody should have to prove how deeply they are hurting.

2. Difficult times reveal human nature

When a crisis disrupts everyday life, people often reveal sides of themselves that remain hidden during more comfortable times. Some respond with kindness and courage, while others become overwhelmed by fear or uncertainty.

Set during a lockdown, Grief Burns Like Fever examines how extraordinary circumstances affect ordinary people and their choices.

The lesson: Difficult situations can test our values, but they can also reveal our capacity for compassion. Even small acts of kindness can make a difference when the world feels uncertain.

3. Human connection matters more than we realise

During periods of isolation and loss, the presence of another person can offer comfort that words alone cannot provide. Feeling understood, supported or simply remembered can make overwhelming circumstances easier to face.

The interconnected lives in Thakur's novel highlight how people can become linked through circumstances beyond their control, even when their personal struggles seem entirely different.

The lesson: Never underestimate the importance of being there for someone. A listening ear, a thoughtful gesture or a little patience can help another person feel less alone.

Also Read
5 Quotes on human connection from the Anxious Generation

4. Sometimes, survival requires finding your own strength

The adolescent in the novel must confront life after his mother's death, while another woman struggles to break free from a situation that has confined her for decades. Their circumstances differ, but both face difficult questions about survival and the possibility of change.

Their experiences invite readers to reflect on the courage it takes to continue when life offers no easy answers.

The lesson: Strength does not always mean being fearless. Sometimes, it means taking the next small step even when you feel uncertain, exhausted or afraid.

5. Hope can exist even in the darkest moments

Grief, fear and uncertainty can make the future appear impossible to imagine. Yet difficult periods do not erase every possibility of change, healing or a new beginning.

Through its exploration of love, longing and human suffering, Grief Burns Like Fever reflects the complicated nature of life during a crisis. People may experience heartbreak and disappointment while still searching for something worth holding on to.

The lesson: Hope does not require you to ignore your pain. It simply allows you to believe that your present circumstances do not have to define every part of your future.

Final thoughts

Grief Burns Like Fever by Minakshi Thakur explores loss, confinement, relationships and survival during a collective crisis, showing how people respond to difficult circumstances.

Thakur is also known for her Hindi poetry collection Neend Ka Akhiri Pul, shortlisted for the Sahitya Akademi Yuva Puraskar in 2012, and her debut novel Lovers Like You and I, shortlisted for the Tibor Jones South Asia Prize in 2013.

The novel's central themes invite readers to look beyond their own experiences and recognise the struggles others may be carrying. Its most meaningful reminder is that even when suffering connects people in unexpected ways, compassion and human connection can help them navigate uncertainty.

item.title: TechSparks 2026: Here’s all that’s happening on Day 2
item.description: Day two of TechSparks 2026 brings Vibecode30, agentic AI, deeptech capital and more, with speakers from Stripe, Swiggy and Peak XV.
item.content:encoded:
Namaskara Bengaluru!

Day one of TechSparks 2026 set the tone for the 17th edition and its theme, ‘The New Tech Order’. On day two, the conversation goes deeper into AI agents, deeptech capital, creativity and the brands of tomorrow.

On October 14, the day opens with YourStory launching Vibecode30 2026, unveiling a cohort that celebrates exceptional technology builders.

Next, Dr Shivkumar Kalyanaraman, CEO, Anusandhan National Research Foundation, Government of India, will share what needs to change for Indian inventions to move from papers and patents into products.

Later, Dr Vignesh Subrahmaniam, Principal AI Scientist, Intuit, will explore what builders need to rethink as AI moves from responding to prompts to reasoning, deciding and acting.

In the afternoon, Chandrika Deb, Country Manager – India, Canva, will reflect on how AI is becoming a co-creator in the creative process. Sanjeev Kumar, CTO, Pine Labs Payment, will unveil three launches built for the agent economy, including an Agent Store for third-party developers.

In a fireside chat, Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director, India, Stripe, will decode how Indian startups can go from early traction to global scale.

Don’t miss the panel representing nearly Rs 2,000 crore in deeptech capital, featuring Vishesh Rajaram (Speciale Invest), Abhishek Srivastava (Kae Capital), Mayuresh Raut (Seafund) and Anirudh Singh (Avataar Venture Partners). They will discuss which technologies investors are most willing to back and where India’s funding ladder breaks.

Rohit Kapoor, CEO, Swiggy Food Marketplace, will talk about the future of India’s convenience economy. In the evening, Mohit Bhatnagar, Managing Director, Peak XV, will discuss how India’s startups can move from valuation to value creation.

On the Focus Stage, Tejas Goenka and Nupur Goenka of Tally Solutions will share how the company has stayed relevant for 40 years. Dr Nagendra Nagaraja, Founder, CEO, and Chairman of QpiAI, will ask whether India is early enough for quantum this time.

The D2C Stage brings together founders and operators on building brands that last, with Natasha Tuli, Founder, Soulflower, and Ananth Narayanan, Founder and CEO, BRND.ME, among them.

Other speakers for the day include Prof Satya Chakravarthy, Founder, The ePlane Company; Deepit Purkayastha, Co-founder and CEO, InShorts; Srijon Biswas, CTO, PhonePe; Dr Geetha Manjunath, Founder and CEO, Niramai Health Analytix; Matt Yi, Co-founder and Tech VP, VeloDB; and Mihir Shah, CBO, Shopflo, among others.

The day also features hands-on Action Labs and executive roundtables with Oppex AI and Stripe.

So, are you ready for round two?

item.title: TechSparks 2026 Day 2: From Krishna Byre Gowda’s Bengaluru blueprint to Stripe’s global playbook, and more
item.description: TechSparks 2026 Day 2: Krishna Byre Gowda on tech-led governance and metro plans, Stripe on going global, VCs on deeptech bets.
item.content:encoded:
On the second day, the 17th edition of TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru moved between policy and product, with conversations on governance, the city’s infrastructure future, global-first startups, and India’s deeptech opportunity.

YourStory’s flagship startup-tech summit brought together founders, investors, policymakers, and technologists to explore how India can build for itself and for the world.

The day’s headline conversation featured Krishna Byre Gowda, Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Government of Karnataka, in a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project. Drawing on his time in the state’s Land Revenue Department, Gowda said technology in governance can minimise corruption and help bridge the trust gap between citizens and the government.

“The more technology we adopt in governance, the better will be our delivery of services to people, and lower will be the levels of corruption,” he said.

He also cautioned that technology alone cannot fix systemic problems without a shift in civic behaviour. Out of an estimated 35 lakh to 50 lakh properties in Bengaluru, he noted, only 23 lakh have registered khatas and just 18 lakh pay property taxes.

The minister also laid out an ambitious plan for the city’s growth. The state government aims to expand Bengaluru’s metro network from 96 km to 170 km over the next 18 months, and hopes to reach 400 km by 2037, the year the city turns 500. Planning is already underway for a 2,000 sq km area around Bengaluru, well beyond the 750 sq km covered by the Greater Bengaluru Authority.

“Hopefully, in the next six months, we can show demonstrable results in making Bengaluru relatively a cleaner city,” Gowda said.

Moving to global ambitions, Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director, Stripe India, said AI is making it faster and cheaper to build world-facing companies from India, giving rise to what he called the “minimum viable company.” According to him, Indian founders can now go global from day one.

He pointed to Emergent hitting $100 million in ARR in eight months, and Stripe data showing 76% of customers prefer paying in their own currency. Maheshwari also confirmed Stripe’s agreement to acquire OpenRouter, which routes AI queries to the most suitable model, a bet on helping companies control fast-rising AI costs.

“In some of the new-age companies, the amount of money people are spending on tokens is more than what they are spending on salaries,” he said.

Deeptech took centre stage in a panel featuring Vishesh Rajaram of Speciale Invest, Mayuresh Raut of Seafund, Anirudh Singh of Avatar Venture Partners, and Abhishek Srivastava of Kae Capital. The investors said deeptech is giving rise to new kinds of founders, driven by India’s talent advantage and the geopolitical push for self-reliance in critical technologies.

Raut said there is still an eight-to-10-year window of opportunity, while Rajaram noted that “nerve and patience” set apart the founders who endure.

Day 3 of TechSparks 2026 will continue to unpack how India can build, own, and scale the technologies of the new tech order. The agenda features conversations on rethinking engineering education with Prof Ashok Jhunjhunwala, building global companies from day one with Omio’s Naren Shaam, AI sovereignty and the next 500 million users, climate innovation in energy, water, and clean air, and India’s $100 billion AI opportunity, before the summit closes with a fireside chat with Zakir Khan.

item.title: Stripe India MD on why Indian startups should build for the world from day one
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director of Stripe India, says AI is making it faster and cheaper to build a world-facing company from India, and that Stripe's OpenRouter deal is aimed at the cost side of the ledger.
item.content:encoded:
Ask Manish Maheshwari what has changed for Indian startups with global ambitions, and his answer is speed. Speaking at the 17th edition of TechSparks, the Managing Director of Stripe India said AI is changing how quickly, and how cheaply, a company can start selling to the world.

"We are seeing the creation of a new way of operating, the minimum viable company," Maheshwari told Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, in a fireside chat on taking startups from early traction to global scale. "The entrepreneurs in India can think global and go global on day one now." The financial infrastructure platform helps companies of all sizes manage their payments.

Maheshwari had examples ready. Emergent, he said, reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR) in eight months, and Pocket FM has recently crossed half a billion in ARR. "If you had asked me two years ago which companies were hitting that level of revenue that fast, I could not have told you," he said.

Stripe's own numbers point the same way. Over the past five years, Maheshwari said, the number of companies using Stripe Atlas, its incorporation and compliance service, to collect money from more than 100 countries has quadrupled. And for most businesses, over a quarter of revenue now comes from outside their top 10 markets.

Stripe, valued at $160 billion and still pre-IPO, pitches itself as the layer that takes the pain out of all this. Maheshwari said founders should not be burning engineering hours on payments plumbing. "As a founder, you want to focus on your core product," he said. "If you are spending your engineering time customising your financial infrastructure, maybe you are not using your engineering in the best way." Stripe's idea, he said, is to make money programmable "through a single API". Founders need not even travel. "You can sit in India and sell to the world, and earn foreign exchange for your country."

Localisation, he argued, is where the money is. Stripe's data shows 76% of customers prefer to pay in their own currency, and that offering local payment methods beyond cards lifts revenue by roughly 12%. "You are leaving 12% of the money on the table by not offering them," he said. It matters for physical goods too, he added, pointing to Purely Copper, which makes copper bottles in India, has built a following in the US, and takes payments through Stripe before shipping.

The OpenRouter bet

Maheshwari confirmed that Stripe has agreed to acquire OpenRouter, a platform that routes AI queries to the most suitable model. The logic, he said, is that AI bills are climbing fast. "In some of the new-age companies, the amount of money people are spending on tokens is more than what they are spending on salaries."

Stripe already helps companies earn money through subscriptions, usage-based billing and invoicing. OpenRouter would help them keep a lid on what they spend. "If you want to build a solid P&L, you need great revenues, but you also have to keep your costs in control," he said. "That is when you make a profit."

Agents and checkout

An audience member asked whether AI agents will finally be able to complete payments on their own. Maheshwari said agentic commerce is "becoming more and more mainstream", at least in the US. He said Stripe's one-click payment product, Link, lets users authorise an agent to spend within a set limit, and that Stripe is helping shape payment protocols for agent-led shopping. "Stripe has a ringside view of this because we are integrated into all the major AI companies," he said. Retailers, he added, are already redesigning their websites so they are "machine readable as well" as human friendly.

item.title: TechSparks 2026 Day 1: Sridhar Vembu, Priyank Kharge, spacetech founders chart India's 'New Tech Order'
item.description: TechSparks 2026 Day 1: Vembu backs tech ownership over GPUs, Kharge pushes Beyond Bengaluru, and Tech30 2026 is unveiled.
item.content:encoded:
The 17th edition of TechSparks opened in Bengaluru with a clear message for India's tech ecosystem: prosperity cannot be imported, and the country must learn to build and own the technologies that solve its own problems.

YourStory's flagship startup-tech summit, themed 'The New Tech Order', brought together founders, investors, policymakers and technologists to examine how India can move from providing technology services to owning foundational technology.

Vembu: Own the foundation before chasing AI

Setting the tone in his inaugural keynote, Zoho Co-founder and Chief Scientist Sridhar Vembu argued that India should prioritise infrastructure and foundational technologies over heavy spending on graphics processing units (GPUs).

"If I earn $10 billion right now, as a government, I will spend the money on Bangalore infrastructure, Chennai infrastructure, all that. There's no point spending $10 billion on GPUs right now," he said.

Vembu said the real obstacle to national prosperity is not the loss of outsourcing jobs but a lack of technology ownership. He claimed that India does 40–50% of Nvidia's chip design work and a large share of software development for Microsoft, Oracle and Cisco, but the financial returns flow to foreign IP holders.

"Ultimately, who has ownership of the technology determines what is the income level of the non-tech people in that economy," he said.

He also predicted major disruption to traditional coding, likening software to a handloom industry about to meet machine looms. By his estimate, AI already writes better code than 60–70% of software engineers and could outperform 90% within three to six months. Rather than lay off staff, he said, Zoho is redeploying engineers to deeptech hardware, including building server infrastructure in-house.

Vembu urged India to follow the path of East Asian economies, building foundational layers first, as China did with Baidu and WeChat. "As much as we think of China as adversaries, I actually look to them as gurus," he said.

Tech30 2026 unveiled

Day 1 also saw Vembu unveil Tech30 2026, YourStory's annual selection of 30 promising startups building India's next generation of technology. He was joined on stage by Yoonmin Cho, APJ Lead, Snowflake for Startups, and Amar Dixit, CEO, WOI India.

Chosen by a jury of ecosystem leaders along with YourStory's senior editorial and research teams, this year's cohort spans spacetech, defence, clean energy, advanced materials, agritech and healthcare. It includes counter-drone maker Apollyon Dynamics, NavIC chip developer MumbaiSemi, quantum-safe encryption startup Pramatra Space, laser-weeding robot maker Harvested Robotics, and Dognosis, which is developing a breath-based cancer screening test.

Kharge: Taking investment to where talent lives

Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home Affairs, IT, Biotechnology and E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, outlined the state's strategy to ease pressure on Bengaluru by bringing investment to where talent already exists.

In a fireside chat with YourStory Founder and CEO Shradha Sharma, Kharge said the Beyond Bengaluru Mission is showing results, with Mysuru delivering close to Rs 4,000 crore in IT exports, Mangaluru close to Rs 3,500 crore, and the Hubballi-Belagavi-Dharwad cluster close to Rs 3,000 crore.

He pointed to recent deals as proof of the policy's reach, including NTT's acquisition of two Udupi-based startups and acquisitions of semiconductor design companies in Belagavi and Mangaluru, some led by founders aged just 23 or 24. The state is also setting up region-specific centres of excellence, including AI centres at IIIT Dharwad and IIIT Raichur, an agritech centre in Kalaburagi and a horticulture centre in Bagalkot.

Spacetech: Building through rejection and failure

The day also turned the spotlight on the gritty reality of building India's private space sector. In conversation with Shradha Sharma, AgniKul Cosmos Co-founder and CEO Srinath Ravichandran and GalaxEye Co-founder and CEO Suyash Singh spoke about surviving hundreds of investor rejections—275 for AgniKul and around 100 for GalaxEye.

Ravichandran explained AgniKul's frugal pay-per-kilogram model, aiming for commercial viability at the $50–60 million mark. "It is more like you give me $500 million and then I will start giving you money back. That is not how India works," he said.

Singh recounted losing communication with GalaxEye's satellite just 30 days after launch, but said such setbacks are part of building the industry. He added that defence is one of the largest markets for space-based Earth observation. "Geopolitics is hotter, and space based surveillance is not an option. It is mandatory," he said.

Both founders flagged the scarcity of growth-stage capital and supply chain hurdles, but remained optimistic that ESOPs and stricter Western visa rules are drawing top engineering talent back to India's deeptech ecosystem.

item.title: TechSparks 2026: meet the innovators exhibiting at India’s premier startup tech summit
item.description: In our photo essay from YourStory's flagship TechSparks 2026 conference, we showcase a range of innovators. Sign up to attend!
item.content:encoded:
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,020 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.

TechSparks is India’s most beloved startup conference and exhibition, organised for the past 17 years by YourStory. In this photo showcase, we feature teams from many startups and ecosystem enablers exhibiting at TechSparks in Bengaluru.

See our earlier exhibitor showcases from TechSparks in 2025,  2024, 2023, 2019, 2018, 2017, and 2016. Also check out our quotes compilations from the conference editions in 2022, 2021, 2020, 2019, 2018, 2017, 2016, 2015, and 2014.

Also Read
Tech in governance can minimise corruption, bridge trust gap between people & govt: Krishna Byre Gowda

The theme of TechSparks this year is The New Tech Order. AI, deep tech and new digital infrastructure are changing how technology is built, who can build it, and how quickly ideas can reach billions.

TechSparks 2026 is about the people, technologies and businesses shaping what comes next, and putting ideas into action. A galaxy of industry leaders, founders and investors are addressing a wide range of questions.

What happens when every business can build its own software? What will India’s next technology advantage be? What does Indian deeptech need to become globally iconic? Does every founder need to build an audience?

Also Read
TechSparks 2026: Here’s all that’s happening on Day 2

In this photo essay, we feature some of the dozens of exhibitors at TechSparks – Startup Park, Sushi Tech Tokyo, PayU, Incred Wealth, Bhasha Bharat, Niti Bodh, Mitra for Life, Feltiv, XSpecies, SearchJob.AI, Pro1 Analytics, Dolphin AI, RentenPe, Aria, Makers Hive, and Rapyder.

Startup Park is an entrepreneurial ecosystem platform designed to help founders turn early-stage ideas into scalable businesses. Its offerings include coworking spaces, innovation labs, incubation programmes, mentorship, networking opportunities, business education, and startup support services.

SusHi Tech Tokyo is an international innovation conference and startup ecosystem initiative led by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government. An abbreviation for the Sustainable High City Tech Tokyo, its focus is on using advanced technology to address urban and societal challenges.

Also Read
New tech order will be built from Karnataka: Priyank Kharge

PayU is a financial technology company that provides digital payment infrastructure to businesses, enabling them to accept and process online payments through multiple payment methods. Its services support merchants with payment processing, transaction management, and related financial technology capabilities for digital commerce.

InCred Wealth is a wealth management and financial advisory business serving affluent individuals, professionals, entrepreneurs, and families. Its offerings include personalised investment strategies, wealth creation, family office services, estate planning, wealth protection, and support for business owners managing complex financial needs.

Mitra for Life is a nonprofit organisation focused on improving access to care, therapy, and inclusion for children and young people with developmental disabilities. Its approach emphasises community-based support, working with families and schools, parent education, specialised therapies, and care delivered closer to where children live.

Also Read
Srinath Ravichandran and Suyash Singh on overcoming failure in spacetech

Feltiv is a technology company focused on AI-powered localization to help businesses adapt content for different languages and markets. Its focus on localisation is relevant to businesses expanding internationally, as well as digital platforms that need multilingual content at scale.

xSpecies is a Bengaluru-based deep-tech robotics company developing physical AI systems that combine artificial intelligence, robotic hardware, perception, and dexterous manipulation. Its technology includes DexteraX, a robotic hand designed for precise object interaction.

SearchJob.AI is an AI-powered recruitment and candidate-assessment platform designed to help organisations identify, evaluate, and hire suitable talent. By using generative AI and data-driven insights, the platform aims to reduce the time and manual effort involved in recruitment while helping employers identify candidates.

Also Read
AI will create new kinds of jobs: Angel One Group CEO

RentenPe is a proptech and fintech platform focused on making residential rental payments more valuable for tenants and more transparent for landlords. By connecting rental history with financial identity, RentenPe aims to address a gap in which regular rent payments do not traditionally contribute directly to a tenant's credit profile.

Makers Hive is an assistive-technology initiative focused on developing affordable solutions for people with disabilities. Its products include KalArm, a mobile-app-enabled bionic hand intended to help people with upper-limb amputations regain practical hand functionality.

Rapyder Cloud Solutions is a Bengaluru-headquartered cloud consulting and technology services company. It helps organisations build, migrate, modernise, and manage their digital infrastructure.

Also Read
Agentic video startup Clueso raises $10M in Series A funding round

Each year, YourStory also presents and felicitates the Tech30 startups. These featured entrepreneurs regarded as having the most promise and potential in India's innovation journey.

Check out our profiles of the Tech50 startups of 2021, and Tech30 startups over the years: 2026, 2025, 2024, 2023, 2022, 2020, 2019, 2018, 2017, 2016, 2015, 2014, 2013, 2012, and 2011.

Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?

(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at TechSparks 2026.)

item.title: Meet the 30 startups shaping India’s tech future; Overcoming failures in spacetech
item.description: At the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks, Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder of Zoho Corp, unveiled and presented this year’s Tech30 at TechSparks 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

From autonomous drones to electric farm machines manufacturers, meet the 30 startups building the next generation of technology. 

At the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks, Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder of Zoho Corp, unveiled and presented this year’s Tech30 at TechSparks 2026. This year’s picks reflect the growing ambition of Indian startups to develop their own technologies and apply them to practical problems. Here’s the full list.

With AI taking over software development, the technology remained the core topic across several discussions at the event. 

“AI already can write better code than at least 60-70% of software engineers out there. And in maybe three to six months, when things accelerate, AI can do better software than maybe 90% of software engineers,” Vembu said, speaking at TechSparks 2026.

But it is not all doom and gloom.

Despite the impending disruption to tech professionals, a huge part of India’s population will remain largely unaffected, said Vembu, presenting a counter-intuitive macro perspective. He pointed out that roughly 97% of the broader population does not write software and operates as consumers of technology.

Meanwhile, the Karnataka government is being cautious about using AI in governance as it first needs to understand how this technology can be used responsibly, Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, said at the event.

However, this does not mean that the state government will not use AI in governance. The minister said the technology is being leveraged for basic issues such as citizen grievances, health, and mobility. He also said the government has set up a committee to study how to use AI responsibly in governance.

ICYMI: All that happened on day 1 of TechSparks 2026.

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • Priyank Kharge on Karnataka’s new tech order
  • Overcoming failures in spacetech

Here’s your trivia for today: Which multinational computer hardware company gets its single-word name from the last four letters of the mythical winged horse Pegasus? (Scroll down for answer)

TechSparks

Priyank Kharge on Karnataka’s new tech order

Karnataka is setting its sights on defining the future of global technology. At Techsparks 2026, Kharge declared that the next era of tech innovation will originate from the state. 

During a captivating conversation with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, the minister highlighted the government’s relentless focus on upskilling local talent to meet the evolving demands of the global economy.

Key takeaways:

  • The minister said that, in the last nine months, the state has attracted close to $4.9 billion investments just from the technology sector. Karnataka’s capital Bengaluru is already the fourth largest technology cluster in the world.
  • He said manufacturing units and global capability centres (GCCs) have come up across the state, and that one of Apple’s supply chain partners operates out of Belagavi, doing precision manufacturing.
  • Kharge added that the state runs dedicated entrepreneurship programmes for startups outside Bengaluru and cited recent deals to emphasise the state’s Beyond Bengaluru policy.

TechSparks

Overcoming failures in spacetech

Building spacetech companies requires nerves of steel, given the nature of the business. Companies have to survive hundreds of investor rejections, acute supply chain bottlenecks, and the constant threat of orbital failure.

Speaking with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks, Srinath Ravichandran, Co-founder and CEO of AgniKul Cosmos, and Suyash Singh, Co-founder and CEO of GalaxEye, shared practical insights into the complex task of building aerospace ventures in an emerging market.

Key takeaways:

  • Ravichandran faced 275 investor rejections before securing initial backing. Singh encountered similar headwinds at GalaxEye, facing roughly 100 rejections.
  • Following a successful test launch in May 2024 using 3D-printed engines and a mobile launchpad, AgniKul is now preparing for orbital customer flights while testing rocket stage reusability, bringing hardware safely back to Earth to lower launch costs.
  • Despite the risks, market demand in spacetech is expanding rapidly. Surging geopolitical conflicts across the globe have made space-based Earth observation indispensable.

News & updates

  • Deeptech: Amansa Investments, SBI Mutual Fund and HDFC Life Insurance Company, and others, have invested over Rs 413 crore in defence electronics maker Tonbo Imaging India Ltd through secondary share transactions, valuing the company at around Rs 4,000 crore.
  • Tech deal: Freshworks has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Torii, a SaaS management platform, as it looks to expand its Freshservice offering into software spend management and AI governance.
  • Fresh capital: Clueso, the agentic video platform for business founded by IIT Madras alumni, has raised $10 million in a Series A round of funding led by Dharana Capital, with Founders Future and Neotribe Ventures joining as new investors.

Which multinational computer hardware company gets its single-word name from the last four letters of the mythical winged horse Pegasus?

Answer: Asus
