item.title: Priyank Kharge on Karnataka’s plans to drive tech growth beyond Bengaluru
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home Affairs, IT, Biotechnology, and E-Governance, Govt. of Karnataka, highlighted the state’s Beyond Bengaluru policy.
item.content:encoded:
Karnataka’s strategy to ease pressure on Bengaluru is to bring investment to where talent already exists, rather than making talent come to where the investment is, Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home Affairs, Information Technology, Biotechnology, and E-Governance, Govt. of Karnataka, said.

The minister was speaking on the sidelines of TechSparks, YourStory’s flagship startup and technology event. In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and Bharat Project, Kharge spoke about the government’s plans to create opportunities for startups and talent beyond Bengaluru through targeted policies, infrastructure and region-specific centres of excellence.

“Because of the government’s constant push on its Beyond Bengaluru Mission and local economic acceleration programmes, Mysuru is today delivering close to Rs 4,000 crore in IT exports, Mangaluru close to Rs 3,500 crore, and Hubballi-Belagavi-Dharwad close to Rs 3,000 crore,” the minister highlighted. 

He said manufacturing units and global capability centres (GCCs) have come up across the state, and that one of Apple’s supply chain partners operates out of Belagavi, doing precision manufacturing. The state has also announced a Bioeconomy Mission covering biotech and agritech, along with related schemes.

Kharge said the state runs dedicated entrepreneurship programmes for startups outside Bengaluru and cited recent deals to emphasise the state’s Beyond Bengaluru policy.

He said NTT acquired two Udupi-based startups for an undisclosed sum. There have also been acquisitions involving semiconductor design companies in Belagavi and Mangaluru.

He added that the founders involved are only 23 or 24 years old.

The government is setting up centres of excellence matched to each region’s strengths, Kharge said. “Wherever there is innovation possible, wherever we are able to ensure that the demography or the talent is good, we are tailor-making policies for that region, and we are ensuring that we accelerate growth,” he said.

“The government is extremely serious about this, which is why we are building centres of excellence based on each region’s geography and demography. We have an AI centre of excellence at IIIT Dharwad and another at IIIT Raichur. We have an agritech centre in Kalaburagi, and we are setting up a horticulture centre in Bagalkot. Wherever innovation is possible and talent is strong, we tailor policies for that region to accelerate growth,” he added.

item.title: Tejas Goenka and Nupur Goenka on how Tally stayed relevant for 40 years
item.description: Tally's Tejas Goenka and Nupur Goenka attributed the company's success to ownership and staying focused on cost, trust and privacy.
item.content:encoded:
Tally Solutions' journey began much before the SaaS, UPI, GST, and startup boom. Founded in 1986, the accounting software company has outlasted several technology cycles and built a customer network of close to three million.

In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, Tally's Managing Director Tejas Goenka and Executive Director Nupur Goenka explained how Tally, a homegrown product company, has stayed relevant over four decades.

Nupur Goenka attributed Tally's success to its focus on ownership. Tally handcrafted its stack from the start, she said, with its own database, its own memory manager, and a programming language invented in-house. The company has rewritten its entire stack five times without carrying over a single line of code.

“The willingness to do that, because you remain uncompromising about your objectives, has been the culture of the company since day one,” she said.

Tejas Goenka stressed on the company' founding principle. "The cost post-purchase should be near zero,” he said, recalling the days when releases were shipped with a support team of one.

Drawing a distinction between being boring and being comfortable, Nupur spoke about the culture of change in the company.

“There’s a tendency sometimes to confuse the boring and successful with the comfortable,” she said. “When you find yourself in any form of comfort zone, it signals unwillingness to change and inertia.” She shared her father’s suggestion to usher in a change every few months to keep the company alive.

On the advent of AI, the Goenkas concurred that the fundamentals will not change: cost, reliability in a business of trust, and privacy. The company uses AI to make Tally useful for founders without compromising customer data.

Tejas talked about a textile manufacturer with revenues of around Rs 1,500 crore where only four people know the customer names. “Imagine giving that data to AI,” he said.

Nupur recalled being told on her first day at Tally that a customer’s data is only the customer’s data. Nobody inside the company has access to it, she said. The challenge is to deliver insights and access to credit without breaking that promise.

The Goenkas also acknowledged the criticism that Tally serves accountants rather than owners. An attempt in 2020 to make changes in its software did not go well. “People threw shoes at me almost,” said Tejas. “We are now not shackled by what was, and we can now make what should be,” he said.

Tejas was candid about the missed opportunities: payroll, which Tally ventured into in Dubai around 2004-05 without finding users, and a retail product it later retired. He still sees payroll as a white space.

Looking ahead, Tejas struck an optimistic note. Tally has made about seven releases in the last three to four years that many customers are yet to discover, and UI changes are due in the coming weeks and months, he said.

Tally is also betting on new geographies, particularly the Middle East and Africa.

“We have an incredible two, three decades in front of us... It would be a shame if we let that opportunity slip to create an impactful technology company out of this country.”

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: Cancellation may be a creator’s biggest turning point: Varun Mayya
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, AEOS Founder and CEO Varun Mayya spoke about how online backlash can free creators to speak their minds, why founders need to get comfortable with reinvention, and why there is no secret formula for going viral.
item.content:encoded:
Building a founder brand is increasingly becoming part of the startup playbook, but finding an audience takes more than posting regularly on social media. It requires years of experimentation, a willingness to stand apart, and the ability to adapt as technology and audience expectations change, according to Varun Mayya, Founder and CEO of AEOS, a content and media-tech company.

Speaking at the closing session of Day 1 of YourStory’s startup-tech summit TechSparks in Bengaluru, the content creator and entrepreneur joined Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, for a fireside chat on building a brand, the secret to virality, and staying agile in an increasingly dynamic content landscape. 

For Mayya, brand building comes down to two things: courage and differentiation. The first is simply having the courage to put yourself out there. He pointed to how comfortable many young Indians, GenZ in particular, are with making videos and sharing them online from their teens, admitting that he didn't have that confidence when he was younger.

Differentiation, for Mayya, is vital. For young founders, standing out can mean raising funding at a time when they have few other markers of success. Securing $5 million or $10 million can set them apart from their peers, give them a story to tell, and offer something to build their social media presence around. While these numbers may matter less once a founder has established a name for themselves, Mayya believes the underlying principle holds: find what makes you different, and build your story around it.

This is particularly challenging in India, where doing things differently invites criticism and consequences. But if founders want to build a distinct identity, Mayya asserted that they need to be willing to take that chance. 

Finding liberation in cancellation

Mayya grew to be more comfortable with criticism after an early experiment with AI attracted backlash. In 2022, he and his team built AutoCode Pro, a GPT-4-powered agent that could write some code and generate Chrome extensions. Seeing how quickly the technology was advancing, he presumptively tweeted that software might not exist in its then-current form four years later.  

The reaction was harsh and instant. In a country where $250 billion of exports comes from software, the tweet struck a raw nerve, and Mayya recalled being widely criticised online. But the experience also changed how he felt about putting his opinions out there.

“Once you've been cancelled, then you can say whatever you want. And I think that has been really valuable. As long as you understand that not everyone’s going to be on your side, then you’re okay,” he said. 

Mayya also spoke about how his content has changed over time. Earlier, he built his voice around serious technology commentary, worrying about what people might think if he mixed in humour or tried something unexpected. Today, he's more comfortable pitching unconventional ideas. 

He suggested that most people start out creating content with their guard up. Their first video is often the ‘LinkedIn’ of themselves, rather than how they might behave in everyday life. Getting comfortable on camera, he argued, involves shedding a protective shell, and giving authenticity a voice. 

He was careful to draw a line. Authenticity is appreciated, but being harmful to others is not. 

The zero mindset: Adaptability in the age of AI

For Mayya, being prepared for uncertainty isn't just about handling criticism. It's also about accepting that a business that works today may not work tomorrow. His approach to business today is what he calls a “zero” mindset. Even a seemingly stable company, he pointed out, can be affected by a platform changing its rules or a new technology disrupting its business model.

“I've now been around long enough to see everyone's stories change. I think the sign of intelligence is adaptation. In our world we see reinvention and pivoting as a bad thing. I'll probably have to pivot again two years later or three years later, and I'm okay with it,” he shared. 

His experience with Aevy TV offers an example of how this played out. The team started with an infotainment channel that mixed information with skits. When the bootstrapped business began running short of money, one of its video editors suggested teaching video editing to generate revenue. The idea worked: students found jobs, and the training initiative grew into a business. The team later moved into content services, working with clients including Zoho, Zerodha, Cleartrip and Vodafone. Eventually, Mayya shared that they became one of the largest editing schools in the world.  

As AI began changing the economics of content production, Mayya set up Aeos Labs to explore how the technology could improve the services business. He shared that the company’s margins had grown from around 10% to nearly 50%. But that improvement comes with a catch. If AI eventually allows clients to do the work themselves, the need for external service providers could vanish. Mayya warned that this puts all large service businesses at risk. 

He also cautioned against making assumptions around AI, saying, “It's not wise to make any final claims against. Earlier I have said AI cannot carry out certain tasks. And then it did.”

In response, Mayya shared that he was exploring offline businesses to diversify beyond digital ventures. Founders need to stay open to changing direction, even when their current business appears to be doing well.

When it comes to viral content, Mayya doesn't believe there's a secret formula to crack. He argued that recommendation algorithms largely reflect what people want to watch. Creators need to understand and mirror what their audience cares about. One approach his team uses is “frame shifting”, which involves connecting a subject to something people are already talking about. For instance, Mayya once reframed a scene featuring jaggery from the movie Dhurandhar to discuss the economics of jaggery production. 

While Mayya shared that his content ecosystem generated around 1.5 billion views in the preceding month, he emphasised that the story was bigger than numbers. It was about adapting, growing and challenging the changeability of the content landscape.

item.title: Bengaluru plans to expand metro network to 400 km by 2037, says Krishna Byre Gowda
item.description: Karnataka Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Krishna Byre Gowda, acknowledged the challenges facing Bengaluru and said there is plan to address some of key issues.
item.content:encoded:
The Karnataka government has ambitious plans for Bengaluru as it seeks to maintain the city’s dynamism while addressing key infrastructure challenges.

During a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, Karnataka Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Krishna Byre Gowda, said, “Bengaluru continues to be the centre for dynamism that nurtures talent and is able to be the home for a lot of people who contribute productively to their own lives, economy and to the services of the country as well as the larger global space.”

The State government plans to create technology spaces, mixed usage locations that will attract knowledge professionals and also investments.

According to the minister, the Greater Bengaluru Authority covers a geographical area of about 750 square kilometers, while Bengaluru's existing urban space already occupies about 1,200 square kilometers. “We are already planning the 2,000 square kilometer space around Bengaluru,” the minister remarked.

Bengaluru’s economic significance is reflected in several indicators. The city accounts for 36% of the new office space created in the country, hosts 40% of India’s global capability centres (GCCs), and contributes around 40-45% of the country’s $300 billion in exports.

Despite the city’s breakneck pace of growth, Gowda highlighted the role of its social ecosystem in sustaining its dynamism.

The minister said the state government plans to expand Bengaluru’s metro rail network from the current 96 kilometres to 170 kilometres over the next 18 months.

“By 2037, Bengaluru will be 500 years old and hopefully by then we can have at least 400 kilometres of metro,” he said.

Besides the metro rail, the State government is also planning to expand the suburban railway network and expand the city's bus fleet. “We do have at least a 10-15 year plan. We are working to crystallize it and put it in place so that it just doesn't remain as a plan on the paper,” the minister said.

The minister acknowledged that Bengaluru faces significant challenges across transport, roads, and civic cleanliness. He noted that these issues should have been addressed at least 25 years ago.

“Hopefully, in the next six months, we can show demonstrable results in making Bengaluru relatively a cleaner city,” the minister said.

Gowda acknowledged the government’s shortcomings and said it was keen to address them. However, he also stressed the need for citizens to change their behaviour, particularly when it comes to waste disposal, to bring about meaningful improvements in the city.

“We understand the sentiment of the people. We acknowledge it. We have a job to do and are taking our job seriously,” the minister said.

item.title: Deeptech is giving rise to new kinds of founders and bold ideas: VCs
item.description: VCs focused on the deeptech segment believe Indian founders have several niche capabilities that can lead to creation of self-reliant technologies.
item.content:encoded:
Deeptech has become a key investing theme in India, and the country's differentiated capabilities has led to the emergence of new kinds of founders, believe venture capitalists focused on this segment.

At a panel discussion at TechSparks 2026, moderated by Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, the panellists were of the view that bold new ideas are coming from founders and entrepreneurs.

Vishesh Rajaram, Managing Partner, Speciale Invest, said, “Everybody's so bold about coming out and doing it. I don't think early capital is going to hold anyone back anymore. I think we will see a lot more innovation coming out of the country.”

In the current context, artificial intelligence (AI) is dominating the headlines, attracting investor interest. The deeptech segment, in particular, offers different kind of opportunities. In addition, the geopolitical environment has created the need for self-reliance in critical technologies.

On the reason for the increased number of deeptech entrepreneurs, Mayuresh Raut, Co-founder & Managing Partner, Seafund, said, “There is still a window of opportunity of eight to 10 years.”

He noted that there were numerous gaps in multiple areas of the deeptech ecosystem, and entrepreneurs need to identify them and come out with the right products.

Anirudh Singh, General Partner, Avatar Venture Partners, cited an example of an India-based radiator company, which is supplying its products across the globe.

He further expounded that in segments like AI and data centres, it will be very challenging for India to match the capabilities of countries like the US and China. But the one advantage that the country has is the availability of talent, he added.

Abhishek Srivastava, General Partner, Kae Capital, noted that given the current geo-political situation it is important to be self-reliant in critical technologies, and this opens up new opportunities.

“It is going to be a bigger opportunity both for investors and founders as the country kind of shapes up for the next few decades,” he said.

The panellists were of the view that deeptech founders must identify niches where they have expertise in and build their solutions around them. The traditional manner of creating products will no longer work, they said.

The VC panellists also highlighted the challenges that deeptech founders will face in their entrepreneurial journey.

Raut remarked that being a startup founder is probably the most arduous undertaking any human can undertake. “These guys (founders) just have an inhuman, almost extraterrestrial ability to just show up the next day, no matter how many knocks they get,” he said.

Rajaram said, “Nerve and patience are two qualities we've seen in the ones (founders) who have outlasted themselves and their businesses.”

item.title: AI will create new kinds of jobs: Angel One Group CEO
item.description: Angel One Group CEO Ambarish Kenghe said demand for knowledge work will go up, and this would require every individual to transform themselves.
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence (AI) will usher in huge transformation and create new kinds of jobs that one cannot imagine now, said Ambarish Kenghe, Group CEO, Angel One.

During a fireside chat at Techsparks 2026 with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, Kenghe did not discount the impact of AI on jobs. However, he was optimistic that demand for knowledge work will go up, and this would require every individual to transform themselves.

He said as AI brings in more efficiency, resulting in higher usage, it could in turn lead to more number of jobs. That is because demand will go beyond what anybody can imagine today, he said. “More jobs will get created but we cannot imagine the kinds of demands that will be placed on human knowledge work,” Kenghe remarked.

On the use of AI in creating wealth, the group CEO of Angel One said the technology has solved for access to various channels that create wealth, but it is yet to solve for information and intelligence.

He believes AI can bridge the wealth divide by providing insights to investors on how they can deploy their capital by taking into account all risks. “If it (AI) is able to provide you with that information, I think it bridges that divide,” he remarked.

Kenghe said institutional investors have the advantages of capital, strategies, and human resources to generate wealth, and AI now has the potential to deliver similar capabilities to retail investors.

On leveraging technology to build products that are simple to use by consumers, he said building a simple product is a complicated process.

“The biggest challenge is finding the right pain point and solving it really well,” he remarked, adding that the more one fails the higher are the chances of success.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: New tech order will be built from Karnataka: Priyank Kharge
item.description: The Karnataka government has initiated numerous programmes to create a talent pool that meets the demands of emerging technologies, said the Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, at Techsparks 2026.
item.content:encoded:
The new tech order will be built from Karnataka, said Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, at the ongoing Techsparks 2026 summit in Bengaluru.

In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, the minister said the state government is focused on building the skill sets required to cater to the needs of the global market.

The minister elaborated the various measures taken by the Karnataka government to expand the skills base in the state. “We have to come up with a programme of ensuring that we build skill sets by the industry, for the industry, of the industry to ensure that people unlearn and relearn technologies that are going to be relevant for the next decade or so.”

The plan will not be limited to the technology sector and also focus also on blue-collar jobs in sectors such as manufacturing, he said.

The minister said that, in the last nine months, the state has attracted close to $4.9 billion investments just from the technology sector. Karnataka’s capital Bengaluru is already the fourth largest technology cluster in the world.

“Forty-three per cent of all tech investments in India come to Karnataka, and this speaks volumes about the availability of talent here,” the minister remarked.

Kharge also highlighted how the talent in the state is engaged in the various centres of excellence (CoE) that the government has created. These CoEs span multiple sectors including agriculture, aerospace, IoT, and AI. The minister said these CoEs have created more than Rs 10,000 crore in market valuation and added that these are run professionally by the industry, with minimum interference from the government.

The Karnataka government's ELEVATE programme provides equity-free grants to startups, and this has now been extended to deeptech startups under ELEVATE Nxt.

As part of Elevate Nxt, the state government provides Rs 1 crore of equity-free grant to deeptech startups focused on solutions for problems faced by citizens. It also provides market access programmes with 40 countries.

“We will be ensuring that we do everything in our capacity to ensure that you succeed as an entrepreneur,” the minister said.

The overall goal is to ensure IP creation, CoEs, state government grants, and local accelerator programmes drive the economic growth of Karnataka.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: 'Govern yourself like HDFC or SBI, build like Google or Amazon': PhonePe's Sameer Nigam
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, the PhonePe CEO said the company's IPO is "hopefully not too far away", outlined its international expansion plans, and explained why governance must keep pace with innovation.
item.content:encoded:
PhonePe Founder and CEO Sameer Nigam said the fintech company hopes to revive its initial public offering (IPO) plans once global markets stabilise, even as it prepares to expand beyond India with a full-stack payments business in the UAE.

Speaking at the 17th edition of YourStory's TechSparks in Bengaluru on Tuesday, Nigam said PhonePe had completed much of the groundwork for its public listing before geopolitical tensions and market volatility forced it to pause the process earlier this year.

"I think hopefully not too far away," Nigam said when asked about the IPO by Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project. "We got our board approvals. We were almost over the line. We'd done our roadshows," he said, recalling how escalating conflicts disrupted the company's plans.

"The first moment of stability, we would like to get back out there," he added, without committing to a listing date.

PhonePe had announced a pause in its IPO plans in March 2026, citing geopolitical uncertainty and volatile market conditions. Nigam declined to discuss the company's potential valuation, saying its draft prospectus reflected the past rather than the future.

Govern like a bank, innovate like big tech

Nigam said payments carry a responsibility other consumer tech does not. "Yes, it's fintech. Yes, it's a consumer tech business. But really, it's a business of trust," he said. PhonePe operates under the oversight of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) and Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) through its various businesses. Nigam said the company undergoes around 130 to 140 external audits annually, roughly once every two working days. "You can't wing it. It has to become a way of life," he said.

His guiding principle is to balance the pace of technology innovation with the governance standards expected of a large financial institution: "Govern yourself like an HDFC or an SBI, build like a Google or an Amazon. Also, in this sector, never switch the two. You'll be dead."

He credited the company's compliance culture to a leadership team that has largely stayed together for a decade and mandatory orientation for every hire, including its roughly 50,000-strong sales network across the country. The message, he said, never changes: "You can't do jugaad at this scale, and ethics are non-negotiable."

UPI for feature phones

PhonePe has taken UPI to feature phones through encrypted SMS-based payments, reviving a technology approach that had initially struggled to gain traction about five years ago, when the industry expected feature phones to disappear. The company subsequently renewed its efforts as smartphone affordability became a growing concern. PhonePe publicly announced its UPI 123Pay offering in August 2026, following its acquisition of Gupshup’s GSPay technology stack in June 2025.

Nigam said job and income losses after COVID, and rising component costs partly linked to demand for AI infrastructure, have made entry-level smartphones increasingly unaffordable for many Indians. "Sales numbers are in decline in India for the first time in 15 years," he said.

The offering, which PhonePe is working to make available across devices from HMD, Nokia, Itel and Lava, is adding around 15,000 to 20,000 users a day, according to Nigam. It has reached about three lakh transactions a month, up from one lakh the month before. "It is growing like a hockey stick on a small base," Nigam said. Users can send money, check balances after direct benefit transfers and receive payments through a UPI QR code. The company is also expanding the range of services, including bill payments and mobile recharges, available on feature phones.

His rationale was simple: "If we are a payments company, our job is to leave no one behind." He added that AI could tackle another barrier, language: "It's not just Bhashini, but conversation will change the game."

Taking PhonePe's payments business overseas

PhonePe has so far enabled Indian travellers to make UPI payments at participating merchants abroad. That falls short in markets such as the UAE and Singapore, where merchants may accept UPI but do not always prominently advertise it, prompting Indian travellers to continue using cards. PhonePe's international CEO, Ritesh Pai, therefore pushed for a broader strategy in the UAE that includes the app, merchant acquiring and remittances.

In September 2026, PhonePe received in-principle approval from the Central Bank of the UAE for two licences covering retail payment services and card schemes, and stored value facilities. Commercial operations remain subject to final regulatory approval. Singapore is the other market the company has applied in, Nigam said.

Nigam hopes others follow. "I would be disappointed if others didn't. We have all the resources. We have all the VCs. We have all the talent. We have all the agency. Now we should go abroad," he said.

Purpose over pay

On AI anxiety, Nigam was sceptical of predictions that technology would fundamentally replace human relationships: "We are not going to get an AI agent as a lifetime buddy and sequester ourselves from mankind." He acknowledged that technological change was disrupting careers and employment, but argued that companies must offer employees a sense of belonging and purpose rather than purely transactional relationships.

To founders, he said money matters less than purpose. "Once you have roots, everything else is a waste," said Nigam, who still lives in the house he moved into 14 years ago. What excites him, he said, is seeing PhonePe QR codes in Leh-Ladakh, Tawang and the Andamans, and the prospect of expanding access to loans from three million people to 30 million. For Nigam, expanding financial access and building sustainable jobs are more meaningful measures of entrepreneurial success than personal wealth.

"That is fun."

item.title: Karnataka govt cautious on use of AI in governance: Priyank Kharge
item.description: The Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Govt of Karnataka, said the government will first look at responsible use of AI before deploying the technology in governance.
item.content:encoded:
The Karnataka government is being very cautious about using artificial intelligence (AI) in governance as it first needs to understand how this technology can be used responsibly, said Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka.

During a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, at Techsparks 2026, Kharge remarked that the state government's cautiousness stems from the fact it owns an enormous amount of data across multiple sectors. “While I keep data privacy as part of the core and use models to develop agents or solutions, governance is very important,” the minister said.

However, this does not mean that the state government will not use AI in governance. The minister said the technology is being leveraged for basic issues such as citizen grievances, health, and mobility. He also said the government has set up a committee to study how to use AI responsibly in governance.

The minister highlighted that the Karnataka government is focused on building the much-needed skill base for AI and is engaged with several companies on this. “One knows how these models (AI) are going rogue; so we are cautious, but at the same time we are investing heavily in skilling,” he said.

“In the next couple of months, one will see a lot of startups and companies working with the government to solve problems,” the minister said.

Also Read
Priyank Kharge on Karnataka’s plans to drive tech growth beyond Bengaluru

The Karnataka government recently came out with a policy to engage with startups to solve certain governance challenges. The minister said it will adopt a sandbox environment wherein startups can build their solutions.

“If they (startups) succeed, I will ensure that it (solution) is taken across the state. But it should be a proven model and, more importantly, it should be solving real-life problems,” said Kharge.

The minister highlighted that startups possess the agility and out-of-the-box thinking to come out with innovative solutions. “I think startups deserve a chance to be with the government,” he remarked.

item.title: Tech in governance can minimise corruption, bridge trust gap between people & govt: Krishna Byre Gowda
item.description: Minister Krishna Byre Gowda champions tech-driven governance to curb corruption and bridge civic trust, urging citizens to share responsibility for Bengaluru’s growth and infrastructure challenges.
item.content:encoded:
Krishna Byre Gowda, Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Government of Karnataka, highlighted technology’s role in improving governance, enhancing transparency, and reducing corruption.

Speaking at a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s annual summit, the minister drew on his previous experience in the state’s Land Revenue Department to illustrate how technology can improve public service delivery.

Gowda said technology-driven solutions could automate government processes, make administration more transparent, and improve public service delivery.

“We implemented a lot of technology-based solutions to completely or partly automate government functioning, make the process a lot more transparent and visible to people, and introduce technology at whatever level possible,” he said, recalling his tenure at the Land Revenue Department.

He said these interventions had significantly improved the government’s ability to deliver results, made processes more transparent, and reduced opportunities for corruption.

“Technology has the ability, if we are willing, to deliver better governance, at least minimise corruption, and be able to meet people's expectations,” said Gowda.

He emphasised that technology can help bridge the trust gap between governments and citizens today. He added that it could do so by enabling governments to respond more effectively and deliver better services.

“I believe—and since I have done it and I could see the results—so now with a lot more confidence, not just as an idea, I can say that the more technology we adopt in governance, the better will be our delivery of services to people, and lower will be the levels of corruption,” he said.

However, Gowda cautioned that technology alone cannot eradicate systemic corruption without a parallel shift in civic behaviour. Stressing that corruption is “not a one-way street,” he noted that “unless two hands meet, the clap doesn’t happen”.

Illustrating the gap in public compliance, he revealed that, out of an estimated 35 lakh to 50 lakh properties in Bengaluru, only 23 lakh possess registered titles (khatas) and a mere 18 lakh pay property taxes. Similarly, on civic issues like waste management, he emphasised that government accountability—such as ensuring daily doorstep garbage collection—must be matched by citizen cooperation, rather than dumping garbage by the roadside.

Addressing the ethical challenges of modern governance, Gowda offered a candid look into political reality.

“In today’s political system, you keep a conscience and try to do the best you can, and don’t sell your soul,” he said, acknowledging that while compromises cannot be entirely avoided, leaders must navigate the system without abandoning their core duty.

Facing steep public scrutiny and administrative friction, he described his daily ethos as simply getting up every morning to “either break your head or break the damn wall” to deliver results.

This administrative push comes against the backdrop of decades of unplanned expansion and infrastructure deficits. Pointing to severe bottlenecks, Gowda noted that planned localities like Jayanagar allocate 23% of their land area to roads, whereas problem-ridden unplanned areas have as little as 8%.

To halt further degradation, the government has stopped new illegal layouts and initiated proactive planning across 2,000 square kilometres—far beyond the current 750-square-kilometre Greater Bengaluru Authority geography—to avoid repeating the mistakes of the past 25 years.

Speaking about the city’s tech ecosystem, Gowda highlighted Bengaluru’s economic weight—the city hosts 40% of India’s GCC investments and generates over 40% of the $300 billion IT service exports.

He urged entrepreneurs and builders to apply their innovation beyond commercial software to real socio-economic challenges, insisting that Indian tech leaders must position themselves at the “head" of the pack—and not follow the pack—to shape the nation’s future.

item.title: The/Nudge secures $15M from Google.org to develop AI tools for small businesses
item.description: Google.org is committing $15 million to The/Nudge to develop AI tools that help Indian small businesses access credit, markets and compliance support, alongside local skills training.
item.content:encoded:
The/Nudge, an Indian action institute focused on livelihoods and economic inclusion, is receiving a $15 million funding commitment from Google.org, Google’s philanthropic arm, to develop artificial intelligence (AI) tools for India’s micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).

The funding aims to improve access to formal credit, market opportunities, and regulatory compliance for small businesses.

The programme will include an open call for proposals to identify practical solutions to business challenges. It will also develop a multilingual, voice-led platform to train people in Tier III and IV towns in job-ready skills and connect them with small businesses.

Google’s announcement estimates that more than 90 million small businesses in India employ over 345 million people, although many continue to face difficulties securing finance and reaching digital markets.

Preeti Lobana, Google India’s Vice President and Country Manager, said the AI technology must address everyday business needs. “For AI to be truly successful in India, it must become a practical multiplier for the millions of small businesses that drive our economic growth,” she said.

The funding comes amid growing investment in technology-led lending to small businesses. In February, Chennai-based Prayaan Capital raised Rs 110 crore in a Series A round led by venture capital firm Peak XV Partners to build a technology-enabled lending platform. In October 2025, Bengaluru-based Optimo Capital raised Rs 150 crore from founder Prashant Pitti and existing investors Blume Ventures and Omnivore, alongside separate debt funding of Rs 110 crore from IDFC and Axis Bank.

Subhashree Dutta, Chief Executive of the^delta, an organisation supporting social entrepreneurs, said the initiative would use “stage-gated grand challenges”, meaning competitive rounds with defined milestones, to support solutions across compliance, market access, quality and credit. She argued that these barriers reinforce one another.

Dutta also said the initiative’s open standards could make MSMEs more competitive, creditworthy and globally visible.

Government initiatives are also targeting the sector’s financing and technology constraints. The IndiaAI Mission, approved in 2024 with an outlay of Rs 10,371.92 crore over five years, supports computing capacity, skills, startup financing, and AI applications. In October, the Union Cabinet approved a separate Rs 10,000 crore SME Growth Fund for direct equity investment in growth-oriented businesses.

Public-sector banks are also using digital credit assessments based on verifiable business data. Official figures show that 98,995 MSME loan applications were sanctioned under this model between April 1 and July 15, 2025.

item.title: Agentic video startup Clueso raises $10M in Series A funding round
item.description: The startup founded by IIT Madras alumni plans to use the funding to scale its enterprise go-to-market reach, deepen its agentic layer, and expand editing capabilities.
item.content:encoded:
Clueso, the agentic video platform for business founded by IIT Madras alumni, has raised $10 million in a Series A round of funding led by Dharana Capital, with Founders Future and Neotribe Ventures joining as new investors.

The round also saw participation from Y Combinator and f7 Ventures. This round brings the total fund raised to $12 million.

Founded in 2023 by Akash Anand, Prajwal Prakash, and Neel Balar, Clueso is based out of California and Bengaluru. It plans to use the funding to scale its enterprise go-to-market reach, deepen its agentic layer, and expand editing capabilities.

The startup says more than 1,000 companies use its platform to create videos for functions such as marketing, customer success and education, onboarding and training. Customers include Atlassian, Zendesk, Gainsight, GlobalPartners, Seismic, and Ironclad. Clueso claims that users have reported productivity gains of over 5x and an 80% reduction in video production costs.

Clueso's co-founder & CEO Akash Anand noted that the company started out by helping customer-facing teams create product tutorials faster. “We quickly saw the same problem across marketing, sales, training and internal documentation. That made us realise the opportunity was much bigger. Today, Clueso acts as an AI video production team that anyone or any team in the organisation can rely on, handling the work of creating, editing and maintaining videos as the business moves.”

Clueso is building AI agents that understand a company’s products, processes, brand and context, and then use that knowledge to create and maintain video across the organisation.

Vamsi Duvvuri, Founder and Managing Partner at Dharana Capital said, “With AI, video is evolving from static media files into living, context-aware assets that continuously adapt as business processes and products change. Clueso is building the infrastructure powering this shift.”

Edited by Swetha Kannan
